claim: Clinical trials are currently underway to assess the efficacy of forniceal deep brain stimulation (DBS) for improvement of memory in Alzheimer's patients.
source: Clinical trials are currently underway to assess the efficacy of forniceal deep brain stimulation (DBS) for improvement of memory in Alzheimer's patients
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published clinical trial reports.

claim: Forniceal DBS has been shown to improve learning and memory in a mouse model of Rett syndrome (RTT).
source: forniceal DBS has been shown to improve learning and memory in a mouse model of Rett syndrome (RTT), an intellectual disability disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in MECP2
evidence: This claim is supported by prior published research from the authors' laboratory.

claim: Rett syndrome is an intellectual disability disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in MECP2.
source: an intellectual disability disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in MECP2
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Rett syndrome etiology.

claim: DBS upregulates genes involved in synaptic function, cell survival, and neurogenesis.
source: We found that DBS upregulates genes involved in synaptic function, cell survival, and neurogenesis
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data and gene ontology analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: DBS normalized expression of approximately 25% of the genes altered in Mecp2-null mice.
source: normalized expression of ~25% of the genes altered in Mecp2-null mice
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data comparing gene expression in Mecp2-null mice with and without DBS treatment.

claim: DBS induced expression of 17–24% of the genes downregulated in other intellectual disability mouse models.
source: DBS induced expression of 17–24% of the genes downregulated in other intellectual disability mouse models
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of DBS-induced gene expression changes with published datasets from other intellectual disability models.

claim: DBS induced expression of genes downregulated in post-mortem human brain tissue from patients with Major Depressive Disorder.
source: DBS induced expression of 17–24% of the genes downregulated in other intellectual disability mouse models and in post-mortem human brain tissue from patients with Major Depressive Disorder
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with published human post-mortem brain tissue data.

claim: Forniceal DBS could benefit individuals with a variety of neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: suggesting forniceal DBS could benefit individuals with a variety of neuropsychiatric disorders
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the overlap of DBS-induced genes with genes altered in multiple neuropsychiatric disorders.

claim: DBS has proven effective in relieving the symptoms of movement disorders, most notably Parkinson's disease and essential tremor.
source: DBS has proven effective in relieving the symptoms of movement disorders, most notably Parkinson's disease and essential tremor (Benabid et al., 1991; Miocinovic et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: DBS was serendipitously discovered to improve memory in a patient undergoing hypothalamic/fornix stimulation for the treatment of morbid obesity.
source: DBS was serendipitously discovered to improve memory in a patient undergoing hypothalamic/fornix stimulation for the treatment of morbid obesity and this further expanded the potential applications of DBS to disorders with impairments in hippocampal memory (Hamani et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published case report.

claim: The safety and efficacy of forniceal DBS to activate the hippocampus is now being assessed in human clinical trials as a therapy to slow the cognitive decline resulting from Alzheimer's disease.
source: The safety and efficacy of forniceal DBS to activate the hippocampus is now being assessed in human clinical trials as a therapy to slow the cognitive decline resulting from Alzheimer's disease (Laxton et al., 2010; Lozano et al., 2016; Ponce et al., 2016; Sankar et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published clinical trial reports.

claim: Forniceal stimulation in mice and rats with defects in hippocampal memory markedly improves deficits in hippocampus-dependent memory tasks.
source: Animal studies have shown that forniceal stimulation in mice and rats with defects in hippocampal memory markedly improves deficits in hippocampus-dependent memory tasks; these improvements correlated with enhanced circuit function and neurogenesis (Hao et al., 2015; Shirvalkar et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior animal studies.

claim: Improvements in memory tasks following forniceal stimulation correlated with enhanced circuit function and neurogenesis.
source: these improvements correlated with enhanced circuit function and neurogenesis (Hao et al., 2015; Shirvalkar et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior animal studies.

claim: Rett syndrome (RTT) is a postnatal neurodevelopmental disorder caused by loss-of-function mutation in the X-linked gene methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MECP2).
source: Rett syndrome (RTT) (OMIM # 312750), a postnatal neurodevelopmental disorder caused by loss-of-function mutation in the X-linked gene methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MECP2) (Amir et al., 1999)
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Rett syndrome etiology, supported by citation.

claim: RTT involves so many gene expression changes in so many neuronal groups that the chance of developing a viable pharmacotherapy seems exceedingly remote.
source: RTT was an intriguing candidate for DBS because it involves so many gene expression changes in so many neuronal groups that the chance of developing a viable pharmacotherapy seems exceedingly remote (Baker et al., 2013; Chahrour et al., 2008; Johnson et al., 2017; Sugino et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple published studies showing widespread gene expression changes in RTT.

claim: DBS improved hippocampus-dependent contextual fear and spatial memory behaviors in both wild-type and RTT mice compared to sham-treated mice.
source: We administered forniceal DBS to awake, freely-moving wild-type and Mecp2-heterozygous mice (a reliable model of RTT), adjusting stimulation intensities in each mouse to ensure we did not trigger seizures, and found that DBS improved hippocampus-dependent contextual fear and spatial memory behaviors in both wild-type and RTT mice compared to sham-treated mice (Hao et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work from the authors' laboratory.

claim: The effect of DBS in the RTT mice was so dramatic that it restored these behaviors to wild-type levels.
source: In fact, the effect of DBS in the RTT mice was so dramatic that it restored these behaviors to wild-type levels
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work from the authors' laboratory.

claim: Improvements in behavior following DBS correlated with increases in long-term potentiation and adult hippocampal neurogenesis, both of which are impaired in RTT mice.
source: These improvements correlated with increases in long-term potentiation (a marker of synaptic plasticity) and adult hippocampal neurogenesis, both of which are impaired in RTT mice
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work from the authors' laboratory.

claim: Forniceal DBS restores hippocampal circuit function in Mecp2-mutant mice.
source: In a subsequent study, we found that forniceal DBS restores hippocampal circuit function in Mecp2-mutant mice (Lu et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work from the authors' laboratory.

claim: Much of neuronal plasticity derives from transcriptional changes triggered by an external stimulus.
source: Much of neuronal plasticity derives from transcriptional changes triggered by an external stimulus, with the genes that respond earliest to neuronal activation encoding transcription factors that set off a cascade of further alterations (Ebert and Greenberg, 2013; Greer and Greenberg, 2008)
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The genes that respond earliest to neuronal activation encode transcription factors that set off a cascade of further alterations.
source: with the genes that respond earliest to neuronal activation encoding transcription factors that set off a cascade of further alterations (Ebert and Greenberg, 2013; Greer and Greenberg, 2008)
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The downstream targets of early response transcription factors encode synaptic proteins and signaling molecules that modulate neuronal synaptic properties.
source: The downstream targets of these transcription factors encode synaptic proteins and signaling molecules that modulate neuronal synaptic properties (Cohen and Greenberg, 2008; Ebert and Greenberg, 2013)
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Activity-dependent changes in alternative splicing contribute to the complexity of the neuronal response by altering the relative abundance of different transcript variants within the cell.
source: Activity-dependent changes in alternative splicing also contribute to the complexity of the neuronal response, by altering the relative abundance of different transcript variants within the cell, which in turn can alter synaptic physiology (Iijima et al., 2011; Mu et al., 2003; Quesnel-Vallières et al., 2016)
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Changes in gene expression at both the gene and isoform levels play important roles in shaping the neuronal proteome in response to stimuli.
source: Thus, changes in gene expression at both the gene and isoform levels play important roles in shaping the neuronal proteome in response to stimuli
evidence: This is an inference based on established scientific knowledge about gene expression and splicing.

claim: DNA methylation is involved in learning and the formation of memories.
source: A growing body of evidence indicates that DNA methylation is also involved in learning and the formation of memories (Feng et al., 2010; Halder et al., 2016; Zovkic et al., 2013)
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Changes in DNA methylation patterns following activity have been observed in the mouse hippocampus and cortex.
source: Changes in DNA methylation patterns following activity have been observed in the mouse hippocampus and cortex, and plasticity-associated genes show an enrichment for activity-regulated methylation sites (Guo et al., 2011; Halder et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2009)
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Plasticity-associated genes show an enrichment for activity-regulated methylation sites.
source: plasticity-associated genes show an enrichment for activity-regulated methylation sites (Guo et al., 2011; Halder et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2009)
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Stimulus-induced alterations in DNA methylation can be correlated with gene expression changes in brain regions.
source: Stimulus-induced alterations in DNA methylation can be correlated with gene expression changes in these brain regions, as well as with discreet aspects of the learning process (Guo et al., 2011; Halder et al., 2016)
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: DNA methylation can be dynamically regulated to influence the behavior of a neuron.
source: These findings suggest that DNA methylation can be dynamically regulated to influence the behavior of a neuron
evidence: This is an inference based on cited studies showing correlations between DNA methylation changes and neuronal function.

claim: 45 min of forniceal DBS with a 20 min recovery period elicited robust activity-dependent gene expression in the DG of WT mice.
source: We optimized the paradigm to acutely activate DG neurons and found that 45 min of forniceal DBS with a 20 min recovery period elicited robust activity-dependent gene expression in the DG of WT mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 1025 genes were either increased or decreased at least two-fold by DBS.
source: 1025 genes were either increased or decreased at least two-fold by DBS (Figure 1C; Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 1C and source data.

claim: Roughly one-third of the genes increased by DBS in WT mice overlapped with genes previously reported to be activity-dependent.
source: Despite these many differences, we found that roughly one-third of the genes increased by DBS in WT mice overlapped with these prior datasets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with published datasets, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Genes upregulated by DBS include many well-characterized immediate early genes such as Fos and Bdnf.
source: these included many well-characterized immediate early genes such as Fos and Bdnf in addition to numerous transcriptional regulators and signaling components
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Gene ontology analysis on the genes upregulated by DBS revealed enrichment in signaling components, transcriptional regulators and anti-apoptotic factors.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis on the genes upregulated by DBS revealed enrichment in signaling components, transcriptional regulators and anti-apoptotic factors (Figure 1D; Figure 1—source data 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: DBS likely leads to transcriptional alterations in many dentate gyrus cell types, not just in mature granule neurons.
source: These findings indicate that DBS likely leads to transcriptional alterations in many dentate gyrus cell types, not just in mature granule neurons
evidence: This claim is based on population-specific expression analysis (PSEA) results shown in Figure 1F.

claim: DBS caused at least a 30% change in expression of thousands of protein coding isoforms.
source: We found that DBS caused at least a 30% change in expression of thousands of protein coding isoforms, and a subset of these isoform expression changes occur in genes whose overall expression does not change, indicating possible isoform switches (Figure 2A; Figure 2—source data 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing isoform analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A subset of isoform expression changes occur in genes whose overall expression does not change, indicating possible isoform switches.
source: a subset of these isoform expression changes occur in genes whose overall expression does not change, indicating possible isoform switches (Figure 2A; Figure 2—source data 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing isoform analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Isoforms that are altered with no overall gene-level expression differences are enriched for proteins associated with neurogenesis, morphogenesis, and synaptic function.
source: GO analysis revealed that these isoforms that are altered with no overall gene-level expression differences are enriched for proteins associated with neurogenesis, morphogenesis, and synaptic function (Figure 2B; Figure 2—source data 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A shorter isoform of Kif1b (isoform 201 with transcript ID: NM_008441) was upregulated nearly two-fold upon DBS, despite the lack of change in overall gene-level expression.
source: We found that a shorter isoform of this gene (isoform 201 with transcript ID: NM_008441) was upregulated nearly two-fold upon DBS, despite the lack of change in overall gene-level expression (Figure 2C)
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing tracks shown in Figure 2C and validated by RT-qPCR in Figure 2D.

claim: The shorter Kif1b isoform lacks a key pleckstrin homology (PH) domain found in the C-terminus of longer Kif1b isoforms.
source: This shorter isoform differs significantly in its protein structure, as it lacks a key pleckstrin homology (PH) domain found in the C-terminus of longer Kif1b isoforms
evidence: This is based on analysis of the protein structure encoded by different isoforms.

claim: PH domains can bind phosphatidylinositol in cell membranes and interact with protein kinase C and heterotrimeric G proteins.
source: Because PH domains can bind phosphatidylinositol in cell membranes and interact with protein kinase C and heterotrimeric G proteins (Wang et al., 1994; Yao et al., 1994)
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about PH domain function, supported by citations.

claim: The shortened Kif1b isoform may have a localization pattern and signaling component interaction distinct from those of the longer isoforms.
source: it is possible that this shortened isoform has a localization pattern and signaling component interaction distinct from those of the longer isoforms
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the structural differences between isoforms.

claim: Many of the observed splicing changes involve synaptic and signaling molecules, including the neurotrophic signaling molecule Bdnf and multiple vesicle trafficking proteins in the kinesin family.
source: Many of the observed splicing changes involve synaptic and signaling molecules, including the neurotrophic signaling molecule Bdnf and multiple vesicle trafficking proteins in the kinesin family
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing isoform analysis data.

claim: Splicing changes in response to DBS make up a large proportion of the RNA regulatory response in neurons.
source: Altogether, we find that splicing changes in response to DBS make up a large proportion of the RNA regulatory response in neurons
evidence: This is an inference based on the large number of isoform changes observed in the RNA-sequencing data.

claim: Many splicing changes likely contribute to the improvements in plasticity and neurogenesis observed in mice that underwent chronic forniceal DBS.
source: many of these changes likely contribute to the improvements in plasticity and neurogenesis observed in mice that underwent chronic forniceal DBS (Hao et al., 2015)
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the types of genes showing splicing changes and prior published observations.

claim: Only a few dozen proteins had more than a 50% difference in levels between sham and DBS samples.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we found only a few dozen proteins with more than a 50% difference in levels between sham and DBS samples (Figure 3—source data 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: Three transcription factors were markedly increased following DBS.
source: Nevertheless, among these differentially expressed proteins we did find three transcription factors that were markedly increased following DBS (Figure 3A; Figure 3—source data 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A number of known targets of the Jun family of transcription factors were altered following DBS.
source: A number of known targets of the Jun family of transcription factors were altered following DBS (Figure 3B)
evidence: This claim is supported by network analysis using the TRANSFAC database, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The Jun-family signaling cascade may be a key player in DBS-mediated transcriptional changes.
source: Many of the transcription factors targeted by the Jun family also targeted genes that were upregulated following DBS, suggesting that the Jun-family signaling cascade may be a key player in DBS-mediated transcriptional changes
evidence: This is an inference based on network analysis results.

claim: The majority of the gene expression changes seen at the acute time point are likely mediated by preexisting proteins in the neurons.
source: It is important to note, however, that while the newly synthesized proteins can contribute to the transcriptional changes we observed, the majority of the gene expression changes seen at the acute time point are likely mediated by preexisting proteins in the neurons
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of protein synthesis versus gene expression changes.

claim: Genes that are upregulated by DBS have lower mCG methylation in their promoters and gene bodies.
source: We found that genes that are upregulated by DBS have lower mCG methylation in their promoters and gene bodies (Figure 4A)
evidence: This claim is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In sham-treated mice, genes upregulated by DBS also show lower mCG levels, suggesting that this lower methylation level is important for the responsiveness of these genes to stimuli.
source: this methylation is lower to start with (i.e., in sham-treated mice these genes also show lower mCG levels), suggesting that this lower methylation level is important for the responsiveness of these genes to stimuli
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that genes with lower baseline methylation are more responsive to DBS.

claim: DBS-induced base-level changes in mCG methylation were overrepresented in exon and promoter regions and depleted in intergenic regions.
source: In comparison with the proportion of the genome falling into one of these four functional categories, DBS-induced base-level changes in mCG methylation were overrepresented in exon and promoter regions and depleted in intergenic regions
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of differentially methylated regions shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Changes in mCH methylation patterns followed the genomic distribution.
source: changes in mCH methylation patterns followed the genomic distribution (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of differentially methylated regions shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Promoter and exon regions may be particularly susceptible to activity-induced changes in DNA methylation.
source: The finding that mCG methylation changes occur at a higher rate than predicted by the distribution of promoter and exon regions in the genome suggests that these locations may be particularly susceptible to activity-induced changes in DNA methylation
evidence: This is an inference based on the enrichment of methylation changes in specific genomic regions.

claim: In the gene Fosl2, decreases in promoter mCG methylation with activity correlated with increased expression of the gene.
source: For example, in the gene Fosl2, whose protein product changed following acute DBS, we observed that decreases in promoter mCG methylation with activity correlated with increased expression of the gene (Figure 4C; promoter region mCG highlighted in yellow boxes)
evidence: This claim is supported by bisulfite sequencing and RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Activity-dependent changes in DNA methylation may contribute to some of the gene expression changes observed post-DBS.
source: These findings suggest that activity-dependent changes in DNA methylation may contribute to some of the gene expression changes observed post-DBS
evidence: This is an inference based on correlations between methylation changes and gene expression changes.

claim: The majority of misregulated genes in KO samples were downregulated.
source: We found that, consistent with other brain regions analyzed in previous studies (Baker et al., 2013; Chahrour et al., 2008; Gabel et al., 2015), the majority of misregulated genes in KO samples were downregulated (Figure 5A)
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data from Mecp2-null mice shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 25% (39 genes) of the genes that were downregulated in KO sham-treated mice were restored to at least WT baseline levels following DBS.
source: We found that 25% (39 genes) of the genes that were downregulated in KO sham-treated mice were restored to at least WT baseline levels following DBS (Figure 5B)
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data comparing KO sham and KO DBS samples shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The rescued genes were enriched for important neural functions, including components of synapses and neuronal projections such as Gad2, Grin2d, and Syt6.
source: These restored genes were enriched for important neural functions, including components of synapses and neuronal projections such as Gad2, Grin2d, and Syt6
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The rescued expression of genes likely contributes to the improved plasticity reported with chronic DBS in Rett mice.
source: The rescued expression of these genes likely contributes to the improved plasticity reported with chronic DBS in Rett mice (Figure 5C; Figure 5—source data 3) (Hao et al., 2015)
evidence: This is an inference based on the types of genes rescued and prior published observations of improved plasticity.

claim: KO mice treated with DBS were capable of upregulating nearly all of the genes increased in WT mice post-DBS.
source: Despite the notable deficits at baseline, we found that KO mice treated with DBS were capable of upregulating nearly all of the genes we found increased in WT mice post-DBS (Figure 5—source data 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of RNA-sequencing data from WT and KO DBS samples.

claim: The level of induction of activity-dependent genes was similar between WT and KO mice.
source: Moreover, the level of induction of these genes was similar between WT and KO mice
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of RNA-sequencing data from WT and KO DBS samples.

claim: Upon DBS treatment, KO and WT samples did not cluster according to genotype in hierarchical clustering analysis.
source: However, upon DBS treatment, KO and WT samples did not cluster according to genotype
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The mean expression levels of most activity-dependent genes are similar between WT and KO samples after DBS.
source: These results suggest that the mean expression levels of most of these genes are similar between WT and KO samples after DBS
evidence: This is an inference based on the clustering analysis results.

claim: Acute stimulation (45 min of DBS with a 20 min recovery period) resulted in the induction of similar activity-dependent genes in female mice.
source: We first established that acute stimulation (45 min of DBS with a 20 min recovery period) resulted in the induction of similar activity-dependent genes in female mice (Figure 6A)
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Only one gene, Rxfp3, was significantly different between WT and Het sham samples at 8.5 weeks of age.
source: Only one gene, Rxfp3, was significantly different between WT and Het sham samples at this early age (female mice were approximately 8.5 weeks of age at time of tissue collection)
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: All four genes assessed showed a significant increase in expression in Het mice following acute DBS.
source: however, we did observe a significant increase in expression of all four gene in Het mice following acute DBS, similar to changes seen in KO mice
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 63 protein coding genes were significantly increased and 94 protein coding genes were significantly decreased in the Het sham samples compared to WT sham samples at 13.5 weeks of age.
source: We found that 63 protein coding genes were significantly increased and 94 protein coding genes were significantly decreased in the Het sham samples compared to WT sham samples (see Figure 6—source data 1 for a complete list of all quantified gene expression changes; mice were approximately 13.5 weeks of age at the time of tissue collection)
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data from chronic DBS samples.

claim: 12 genes that were downregulated in Het sham samples were significantly upregulated (fold-change >15%, FDR < 0.05) following chronic DBS in the Het samples.
source: We found that 12 of these genes were significantly upregulated (fold-change >15%, FDR < 0.05) following chronic DBS in the Het samples (Figure 6C; genes with a significant increase in expression are indicated by asterisks)
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Het DBS samples show a trend toward improved expression of both up- and downregulated genes.
source: Further, when we looked at the average expression of genes that are significantly altered in Het sham samples (protein coding genes that are either up- or downregulated by at least 20%, FDR < 0.05), we found that Het DBS samples show a trend toward improved expression of both up- and downregulated genes
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Three of the four Het DBS samples cluster with the WT samples in hierarchical clustering analysis.
source: three of the four Het DBS samples even cluster with the WT samples (Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nearly 23% (185 genes) of the genes that are downregulated in the hippocampus of Ptchd1-KO mice are amongst the genes that increase following DBS in WT mice.
source: We found that nearly 23% (185 genes) of the genes that are downregulated in the hippocampus of Ptchd1-KO mice are amongst the genes that increase following DBS in WT mice (Figure 7A)
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with published gene expression data from Ptchd1-KO mice.

claim: Nearly 24% (22 genes) of the genes that are downregulated in Rsk2-KO mice are upregulated by forniceal DBS.
source: Similarly, a dataset derived from a mouse model of Coffin-Lowry syndrome (OMIM # 303600), a syndromic form of intellectual disability caused by loss-of-function mutations in the RPS6KA3 gene which encodes RSK2, also showed that nearly 24% (22 genes) of the genes that are downregulated in Rsk2-KO mice are upregulated by forniceal DBS (Figure 7A)
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with published gene expression data from Rsk2-KO mice.

claim: 17% (325 genes) of the genes that are decreased in expression in the dentate gyrus of patients with MDD are upregulated by forniceal DBS.
source: Again, we found a small but significant overlap between this dataset and DBS-upregulated genes, with 17% (325 genes) of the genes that are decreased in expression in the dentate gyrus of patients with MDD being upregulated by forniceal DBS (Figure 7A)
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with published gene expression data from human MDD patients.

claim: The overlaps between intellectual disability/MDD datasets and DBS-induced genes are significant and not due to chance.
source: We were surprised to find that a substantial number of genes in each of these disorders were induced by DBS in WT mice, and that the overlaps between these datasets and DBS-induced genes are significant and not due to chance (Fisher exact test; p<0.001)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis using Fisher's exact test.

claim: Few genes were shared among all of the disorders in the overlap with DBS data.
source: Further, when we assessed which genes were found in the overlap between these datasets and the DBS data, we saw that few genes were shared among all of the disorders (Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The potential transcriptional benefits of DBS would be different for each disorder.
source: indicating that the potential transcriptional benefits of DBS would be different for each disorder
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that different genes overlap between DBS and different disorders.

claim: Approximately 35% (237 genes) of genes upregulated by fluoxetine treatment are also upregulated by DBS.
source: When we compared the genes that were upregulated by fluoxetine treatment, we found that approximately 35% (237 genes) are also upregulated by DBS (Figure 7B)
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with published gene expression data from fluoxetine-treated mice.

claim: Nearly 22% (166 genes) of the genes upregulated after 4 days of running are also increased post-DBS.
source: Nearly 22% (166 genes) of the genes upregulated after 4 days of running are also increased post-DBS (Figure 7B)
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with published gene expression data from running mice.

claim: The overlap between DBS and fluoxetine/running datasets is significant.
source: In both comparisons, the overlap with DBS is significant (Fisher exact test; p<0.001)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis using Fisher's exact test.

claim: DBS utilizes some of the same transcriptional programs activated by fluoxetine and running.
source: These findings suggest that DBS utilizes some of the same transcriptional programs activated by fluoxetine and running
evidence: This is an inference based on the significant overlap of gene expression changes.

claim: Forniceal DBS induces changes in the expression of thousands of genes and splice variants.
source: We found that forniceal DBS induces changes in the expression of thousands of genes and splice variants
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Many DBS-induced gene expression changes are in genes that have been previously reported to be activity-dependent.
source: many of these changes are in genes that have been previously reported to be activity-dependent (Eom et al., 2013; Flavell et al., 2008; Halder et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2008; Madabhushi et al., 2015; Xiang et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with published activity-dependent gene expression datasets.

claim: The finding that many genes in the DBS dataset overlap with genes upregulated by environmental enrichment suggests that DBS acts through physiological pathways involved in plasticity.
source: The finding that many genes in the DBS dataset overlap with genes upregulated by environmental enrichment (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1) suggests that DBS acts through physiological pathways involved in plasticity
evidence: This is an inference based on the overlap with environmental enrichment gene expression data.

claim: The observation that a significant proportion of DBS-induced genes are involved in regulation of apoptosis hints that DBS is supporting the survival of either existing DG neurons or of newly born neurons in the subgranular zone.
source: The observation that a significant proportion of DBS-induced genes are involved in regulation of apoptosis is particularly interesting, as it hints that DBS is supporting the survival of either existing DG neurons or of newly born neurons in the subgranular zone
evidence: This is an inference based on gene ontology analysis results.

claim: Forniceal DBS influences gene expression in mature granule cells and in cycling cells in the dentate gyrus.
source: This indicates that forniceal DBS not only influences gene expression in mature granule cells but in cycling cells in the dentate gyrus
evidence: This is an inference based on population-specific expression analysis results.

claim: The finding that numerous genes are differentially expressed following DBS specifically in neuroprogenitor cells helps explain why neurogenesis is strongly enhanced following chronic forniceal DBS.
source: This finding also helps explain why neurogenesis is strongly enhanced following chronic forniceal DBS (Hao et al., 2015)
evidence: This is an inference based on population-specific expression analysis and prior published observations.

claim: Further studies are needed to determine if neurogenesis is required for the behavioral improvement observed post-DBS.
source: To better understand the mechanisms of action of forniceal DBS, further studies are needed to determine if neurogenesis is required for the behavioral improvement observed post-DBS
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: Many isoforms have yet to be characterized in terms of their function, localization, and/or interactor differences.
source: Although many isoforms have yet to be characterized in terms of their function, localization, and/or interactor differences
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge.

claim: Many of the isoforms detected have unique features within their protein coding regions, suggesting that these isoforms play distinct roles from other isoforms of the same gene.
source: many of the isoforms we detected do have unique features within their protein coding regions, suggesting that these isoforms play distinct roles from other isoforms of the same gene
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis of the detected isoforms.

claim: More work is needed to better understand the functional consequences of splicing changes and their overall influence on neurons.
source: More work is needed to better understand the functional consequences of these splicing changes and their overall influence on neurons
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: A subset of transcription factors are among the first proteins altered following DBS, including a number of Jun-family transcription factors.
source: Our proteomics data revealed that a subset of transcription factors are among the first proteins altered following DBS, including a number of Jun-family transcription factors
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: Some proteins may have been overlooked in the proteomics analysis due to limitations in the number of proteins that can be confidently identified.
source: However, given the limitations in terms of the number of proteins that can be confidently identified in a given sample, we cannot rule out the possibility that some proteins may have been overlooked in our analysis
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the mass spectrometry method.

claim: The list of Jun-family transcription factor targets is likely to underestimate the actual number of genes regulated by these transcription factors.
source: This list of targets is still likely to underestimate the actual number of genes regulated by these transcription factors, as the TRANSFAC database, which contains validated interactions, is not an exhaustive list of all targets
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the TRANSFAC database.

claim: Newly synthesized Jun-family proteins help to augment the transcriptional cascade mediated by already existing Jun family proteins within the cell.
source: These newly synthesized proteins help to augment the transcriptional cascade mediated by already existing Jun family proteins within the cell
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of transcription factors.

claim: Newly synthesized Jun-family proteins may serve as activity-dependent epigenetic regulators.
source: may also serve as activity-dependent epigenetic regulators (Su et al., 2017)
evidence: This is based on a cited study showing that Jun-family proteins can act as epigenetic regulators.

claim: Neuronal activity can influence chromatin accessibility and Junb and Fos are enriched at newly opened chromatin regions.
source: A recent study found that neuronal activity can influence chromatin accessibility and Junb and Fos are enriched at these newly opened regions (Su et al., 2017)
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from a cited study.

claim: Newly synthesized Jun-family proteins may act to reshape the chromatin landscape to influence later phases of activity-dependent gene expression.
source: Thus, these newly synthesized proteins may also act to reshape the chromatin landscape to influence later phases of activity-dependent gene expression
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of Jun-family proteins in chromatin remodeling.

claim: The methylation patterns observed belong predominantly to granule neurons because the dentate gyrus is comprised primarily of granule neurons.
source: Because the dentate gyrus is comprised primarily of granule neurons (Guo et al., 2011), the methylation patterns we observed belong predominantly to this neuronal subtype
evidence: This is an inference based on the cellular composition of the dentate gyrus.

claim: A subset of the DNA methylation changes may result from changes in other dentate cell types.
source: However, we cannot exclude the possibility that a subset of the DNA methylation changes we identified result from changes in other dentate cell types
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging a limitation of the analysis.

claim: Lowered mCG methylation on gene promoters and gene bodies provides a priming effect, enabling rapid gene expression increases.
source: Further, mCG levels were lower on these genes in both sham and DBS samples, suggesting that lowered methylation provides a priming effect, enabling rapid gene expression increases
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between low methylation and gene responsiveness to DBS.

claim: Alterations in mCG density did not tend to fall within the genes with the greatest alterations in expression post-DBS.
source: Alterations in mCG density were overrepresented in exon and promoter regions, yet these changes did not tend to fall within the genes with the greatest alterations in expression post-DBS
evidence: This is an observation from the DNA methylation analysis.

claim: DNA methylation changes may occur in genes whose expression rises at later time points.
source: An interesting possibility is that these methylation changes occur in genes whose expression rises at later time points
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the timing of gene expression changes.

claim: mCH may have less of a direct role in activity-dependent gene expression changes than mCG.
source: These findings suggest that mCH may have less of a direct role in activity-dependent gene expression changes
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mCH changes follow genomic distribution.

claim: Changes in both mCG and mCH levels in intergenic regions may affect the activity of enhancer regions, thereby indirectly influencing gene expression.
source: It may be, however, that the changes we see in both mCG and mCH levels in intergenic regions affect the activity of enhancer regions, thereby indirectly influencing gene expression
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential role of intergenic methylation changes.

claim: MeCP2 is not required for DBS-induced activity-dependent gene expression in the dentate gyrus.
source: These data unequivocally show that MeCP2 is not required for DBS-induced activity-dependent gene expression in the dentate gyrus: KO mice are capable of activating the same transcriptional programs following DBS as WT mice
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data showing similar gene expression responses in WT and KO mice following DBS.

claim: The finding that MeCP2 is not required for DBS-induced transcription is consistent with the methylation data showing that genes upregulated by DBS have lower baseline mCG methylation levels.
source: The finding that MeCP2 is not required for DBS-induced transcription is also consistent with the methylation data we gathered. Genes that are upregulated by DBS have lower baseline mCG methylation levels. Thus, MeCP2 is less likely to bind to these genes and contribute to the regulation of their expression
evidence: This is an inference connecting the gene expression and methylation data.

claim: MeCP2 is less likely to bind to genes with lower mCG methylation levels.
source: Genes that are upregulated by DBS have lower baseline mCG methylation levels. Thus, MeCP2 is less likely to bind to these genes and contribute to the regulation of their expression
evidence: This is based on established knowledge that MeCP2 binds to methylated DNA.

claim: One of the likely benefits of DBS in Mecp2-null mice is the rescue of abnormal expression of synaptic proteins.
source: In addition to upregulating normal activity-dependent gene expression paradigms in KO mice, one of the likely benefits of DBS in Mecp2-null mice is the rescue of abnormal expression of synaptic proteins
evidence: This is an inference based on the types of genes rescued by DBS in KO mice.

claim: Perturbations in the balance between inhibitory and excitatory signaling in MeCP2 mouse models has been well established.
source: These genes are of particular interest because perturbations in the balance between inhibitory and excitatory signaling in MeCP2 mouse models has been well established
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Rett syndrome mouse models.

claim: Both GABA synthesis and NMDA receptor signaling have been implicated in the circuit dysfunction observed in MeCP2 mouse models.
source: both GABA synthesis and NMDA receptor signaling have been implicated in the circuit dysfunction observed in these mice (Calfa et al., 2015; Chao et al., 2010; Chao et al., 2007; Ure et al., 2016)
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Enhanced transcription and neurogenesis likely contribute to the improvements in learning and memory observed following chronic DBS in Rett mice.
source: This enhanced transcription and neurogenesis likely contribute to the improvements in learning and memory observed following chronic DBS in Rett mice
evidence: This is an inference based on the types of genes rescued and prior published behavioral observations.

claim: 17 days after chronic DBS was completed, normalization of Gad2 and a handful of other signaling molecules was observed in Mecp2-heterozygous female mice.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis are our findings of sustained transcriptional rescue in Mecp2-heterozygous female mice weeks after chronic forniceal DBS treatment ended. It is notable that 17 days after DBS was completed, we observed normalization of Gad2 and a handful of other signaling molecules
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data from chronic DBS samples.

claim: More genes would likely be significantly rescued if transcription was assessed at an earlier time point post-chronic DBS.
source: While many genes show a trend toward rescued expression in Het DBS samples, we predict that more genes would be significantly rescued if we assessed transcription at an earlier time point post-chronic DBS, as the restoration of normal gene expression likely tapers off over time
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the observation that gene rescue effects may diminish over time.

claim: Repeating forniceal stimulation every few weeks throughout life would be necessary to maintain the effects of its benefits in dentate neurons.
source: Thus, repeating forniceal stimulation every few weeks throughout life would be necessary to maintain the effects of its benefits in dentate neurons
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that gene expression changes taper off over time after DBS ends.

claim: Forniceal DBS holds therapeutic promise for other diseases where hippocampal function is disrupted.
source: Forniceal DBS holds therapeutic promise for other diseases where hippocampal function is disrupted
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the overlap of DBS-induced genes with genes altered in other disorders.

claim: SSRI-resistant patients with major depressive disorder may benefit from DBS.
source: These findings suggest that SSRI-resistant patients with major depressive disorder may benefit from DBS, as this treatment is able to both induce expression of genes that are downregulated in these patients as well as upregulate many of the same genes induced by fluoxetine treatment
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the overlap of DBS-induced genes with genes altered in MDD and by fluoxetine.

claim: The vast number of different genetic changes involved in intellectual disabilities and neuropsychiatric disorders makes it hard to imagine that a drug-based treatment could be effective.
source: The vast number of different genetic changes involved in intellectual disabilities and neuropsychiatric disorders makes it hard to imagine that a drug-based treatment could be effective
evidence: This is an inference based on the complexity and heterogeneity of intellectual disabilities.

claim: DBS has proven safe in humans.
source: Although considered an invasive treatment, DBS has proven safe in humans
evidence: This is established knowledge from clinical use of DBS.

claim: DBS could offer therapeutic options for otherwise untreatable intellectual disability disorders.
source: DBS has proven safe in humans and could offer therapeutic options for these otherwise untreatable disorders
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential therapeutic application of DBS.
